items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's take a look at the function [MATH: y=\dfrac 1 x] below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ced7d425b27c52b44b231c6ae73fb83b]

Content:
The function has a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=0.] There is also a discontinuity in the function at [MATH: x=0,] since we cannot draw the points on the curve without taking our pen off the paper to cross the asymptote.

Content:
So, we say that [MATH: y = \dfrac 1 x] has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=0.] Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called infinite discontinuities.

Content:
Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty.]

Content:
In general, a function [MATH: y=f(x)] has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=c] if either one-sided limit is infinite:

Content:
[MATH: \lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty.]

Content:
Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at [MATH: x=c.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The function has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes at [MATH: x=\pm 1.] Note that

[MATH: \lim_{x\to (-1)^{+}} f(x) = -\infty,]

which is enough to conclude that there is a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=-1.] Similarly

[MATH: \lim_{x\to 1^{-}} f(x) = \infty,]

which is enough to conclude that there is a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at [MATH: x=1.]

There is also a discontinuity at [MATH: x=-2,] but this is a point discontinuity, not a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote.

items.title: Finding Infinite Discontinuities of Rational Functions

sections.normalized_html: Find all the points where the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2-5x+6}] has infinite discontinuities.
sections.readable_text: Find all the points where the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{1}{x^2-5x+6}] has infinite discontinuities.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of [MATH: y=f(x).]

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expression in the denominator. This gives

[MATH: f(x)|= (1)/(x^{2} − 5x + 6); = (1)/((x − 3)(x − 2)).]

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we can find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator to zero:

[MATH: (x-3)(x-2) = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=2,3.]

Therefore, the function has infinite discontinuities at [MATH: x=2] and [MATH: x=3.]

sections.normalized_html: Find all the points where the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+x-6}{x^2-4}] has infinite discontinuities.
sections.readable_text: Find all the points where the function [MATH: f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+x-6}{x^2-4}] has infinite discontinuities.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of [MATH: y=f(x).]

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expressions in the numerator and denominator. This gives

[MATH: f(x)|= (x^{2} + x − 6)/(x^{2} − 4); = ((x − 2)(x + 3))/((x − 2)(x + 2)); = ((x − 2)(x + 3))/((x − 2)(x + 2)); = (x + 3)/(x + 2).]

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

[MATH: x+2 = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=-2.]

Therefore, the function has an infinite discontinuity at [MATH: x=-2.]

items.title: Finding Infinite Discontinuities of a Piecewise Function

sections.normalized_html:
Find all of the points where [MATH: f(x)] below has infinite discontinuities.

[MATH: {(1)/(x − 5),|x < 5; (1)/(x − 4),|x ≥ 5.]
sections.readable_text:
Find all of the points where [MATH: f(x)] below has infinite discontinuities.

[MATH: {(1)/(x − 5),|x < 5; (1)/(x − 4),|x ≥ 5.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of [MATH: y=f(x).] The only possible way that [MATH: y=f(x)] can have vertical asymptotes is if either [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-5}] or [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-4}] grow without bound within their respective subdomains.

  • We first compute the asymptotes of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-5}.] Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get [MATH: x-5=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=5.] Although this branch of the function is defined for [MATH: x < 5], we do have that [MATH: \lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-5}\right) = -\infty,] and therefore we conclude that [MATH: x=5] is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

  • Next, we compute the asymptotes of [MATH: \dfrac{1}{x-4}.] Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get [MATH: x-4=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=4.] However, this branch of the function is defined for [MATH: x \geq 5,] which does not contain the neighborhood of [MATH: x=4.] So [MATH: x=4] cannot be a vertical asymptote, and therefore [MATH: x=4] cannot be an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, the function [MATH: f(x)] only has a single infinite discontinuity, and it is at [MATH: x=5.]

This matches up with what we see in the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] shown below.

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expressions in the numerator and denominator. This gives

[MATH: f(x)|= (x^{2} + x − 6)/(x^{2} − 4); = ((x − 2)(x + 3))/((x − 2)(x + 2)); = ((x − 2)(x + 3))/((x − 2)(x + 2)); = (x + 3)/(x + 2).]

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:
